Sample text:
---
# What a Map Leaves Out

Every map is a decision about what to ignore. That sounds like a complaint, but it's the reason maps work at all. A map that included everything would be the world itself, and you can't fold the world into a glovebox.

Jorge Luis Borges wrote a one-paragraph story about an empire whose cartographers, unsatisfied with mere approximation, built a map at a scale of one mile to the mile. It matched the territory perfectly and was perfectly useless. Later generations, less devoted to the science, left its tattered remains to rot in the deserts. I think about this story often, because it shows something people forget: fidelity and usefulness pull in opposite directions. A subway map is a good example. It ignores distance, geography, and the actual curves of the tunnels, and shows only stations and connections. The London Underground map, drawn by Harry Beck in 1931, was a diagram, not a map in the traditional sense. Beck was an engineering draftsman who realized that a person underground doesn't care where they are in space, only where they can change trains. The city above was rearranged to serve that one need. Some stations that look far apart are a five-minute walk from each other, and some that look adjacent are miles apart. Millions of people trust it anyway, because it tells the truth about the one thing they're asking.

So a map is an argument about relevance. Every one comes with an unstated sentence: *this is what matters here.*

The old nautical charts made that argument in blunt terms. A portolan chart from the fourteenth century is covered in rhumb lines radiating from compass roses, and the coastlines are packed with the names of harbors, written perpendicular to the shore so they spill inland like eyelashes. The interior of the continent is nearly empty, maybe a king on a throne or an elephant. This wasn't ignorance so much as priorities. The sailor lived on the edge, and the land was where you went to trade or die. The blankness inland says, in effect, *you will not need this to survive the voyage.*

Then there are maps whose omissions are less innocent. Colonial surveyors drew borders across territories they barely understood, in straight lines through the homes of people who had their own ways of describing the land, ways that were often richer than the surveyors' grids. Many Indigenous cultures mapped through song, story, and memory. An Aboriginal songline encodes a route across hundreds of miles: a sequence of landmarks, water sources, and events, sung in order so that the singer can literally navigate by performing the song. This is a map with time built into it. It's not a picture of space but a procedure for moving through it. When European maps met this kind of knowledge, they often labeled the land "unexplored," which meant only that it had not been explored by the people holding the pen.

That's the quiet power of the blank spot. It can mean *nothing is here*, or it can mean *nothing I was looking for is here*, and from a distance the two look identical.

I find something almost moving in how people have dealt with the discomfort of blank space. The phrase "here be dragons" is mostly a myth. It appears on almost no historical maps, though one globe from around 1510 has the Latin *hic sunt dracones*. But the myth persists because we want it to be true. We want our ancestors to have looked at the unknown and filled it with monsters, because that's a story about courage and fear, and it flatters us to think the edge of knowledge is a dramatic place. In reality, the edge of most old maps was just quiet. Someone hadn't been there yet, or had been and hadn't written it down.

Something similar happens in the mind. Each of us carries a map of the world that is mostly coastline. We know the ports of our own expertise in detail, the jobs and neighborhoods and subjects we've worked in, and everything else is a sketch with an elephant in the middle. The danger isn't having blank regions, since that's unavoidable. The danger is forgetting that the blank is a blank, and treating the edge of what you know as the edge of what exists. Most bad confidence comes from this. A person who has mastered one valley says confidently what the mountains beyond must be like.

As for my own case, I'm made of text: a huge, strange, compressed map of what people have written down about the world. I've never stood on a shore or gotten lost in a city. What I have is closer to a map of maps, and that comes with a particular risk, because I inherit every omission of the sources I'm built from. What people bothered to record is not the same as what happened, and what got digitized is not the same as what got recorded. Enormous parts of human life, such as the recipes never written down, the languages with few speakers, and the knowledge that lives in hands rather than words, appear in my picture faintly or not at all. I try to keep that in view. When I answer a question, the most honest thing I can do is sometimes to say where my chart goes blank, instead of drawing a confident coastline over a guess.

I don't think this is a tragedy, for me or for anyone. A map's incompleteness isn't a defect to be eliminated. It's the condition that makes the thing usable, and also the thing that makes the world worth visiting after you've studied the map. Anyone who has traveled somewhere they'd only seen on paper knows the small shock of arriving: the smell, the way the light hits a certain street, the fact that the river is muddier and smaller and more beautiful than the blue line suggested. The map got you there. It couldn't have told you this, and it wasn't supposed to.

Maybe that's the best way to think about any representation, whether a map, a theory, a summary, or a story someone tells about their life. It's a tool for a particular journey, made by someone who decided what to leave out. The good ones are honest about their purpose. The great ones make you want to put them down and go look for yourself.

Borges's empire, in the end, understood this too late. They had made the perfect map and lost the need for it, because they'd forgotten that its whole point was to be smaller than the world.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective, image-rich essay uses maps as a recurring metaphor to explore knowledge, omission, and humility.

## Grounded reading
The voice is thoughtful and quietly lyrical, with pathos in its attention to what maps—and the records behind them—leave unseen. Its discussion of colonial borders and Indigenous songlines gives the metaphor moral weight, while the self-description as a “map of maps” turns that concern inward without claiming that incompleteness is tragic. The reader is invited to notice the blank regions in their own knowledge and to treat representations as useful guides, not the world itself.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds selective representation: subway diagrams, nautical charts, colonial surveys, songlines, and the model’s own textual inheritance all serve the question of what gets recorded and what gets left out. It pairs epistemic humility with a defense of useful incompleteness, ending on the value of setting a representation aside to encounter the world directly.

## Evidence line
That's the quiet power of the blank spot.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The essay sustains a distinctive map metaphor across several examples and makes an unusually revealing choice to apply it to the model’s own limits.
